On January 1, 1801, the first asteroid, Ceres, was discovered, and just a month later, it was lost again behind the glare of the sun. Astronomers faced the challenge of calculating Ceres' orbit months into the future using only 22 observations. Being the first object of its kind to be discovered, astronomers did not know what eccentricity its orbit should have. Many tried guessing based on their "expertise," but Gauss solved the problem purely empirically - by analyzing data and making no further assumptions beyond Kepler's laws. 

Gauss ended up with the best estimate - the asteroid was rediscovered exactly where he predicted - and became the OG data scientist. In the process, he invented the method of maximum likelihood estimation, (not so) ordinary least squares, applied it to linear regression, and discovered his most enduring legacy - *the bell curve* (and some astronomy stuff). In this class, we will learn all of these things (not the astronomy stuff). 

```{python}
import numpy as np 
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

# Piazzi's observations
t_days = np.array([0, 1, 2, 3, 6, 7, 8, 10, 11, 12, 13, 14, 16, 18, 20, 22, 
                   31, 35, 37, 39, 40, 41])

RA_deg = np.array([51.797, 52.070, 52.344, 52.618, 53.714, 53.988, 54.261,
                   54.809, 55.083, 55.357, 55.630, 55.904, 56.452, 56.999,
                   57.547, 58.096, 60.640, 62.182, 63.189, 64.197, 64.700, 65.204])

Dec_deg = np.array([16.133, 16.408, 16.682, 16.956, 17.779, 18.053, 18.327,
                    18.874, 19.148, 19.422, 19.695, 19.968, 20.513, 21.058,
                    21.602, 22.146, 23.642, 24.172, 24.416, 24.610, 24.688, 24.766])

# ============ FIGURE 1 & 2: Side by Side ============
fig = plt.figure(figsize=(16, 6))

# LEFT: Detail View
ax1 = fig.add_subplot(121)

# Plot trajectory
ax1.scatter(RA_deg, Dec_deg, c=t_days, cmap='plasma', 
       s=150, edgecolors='black', linewidth=0, zorder=3)

# Add observation numbers
for i, (ra, dec, day) in enumerate(zip(RA_deg, Dec_deg, t_days)):
    ax1.annotate(f'{i+1}', (ra, dec), 
          fontsize=8, ha='center', va='center', 
          color='white', fontweight='bold')

# Add date labels for key observations
key_dates = [(0, 'Jan 1'), (10, 'Jan 11'), (15, 'Jan 23'), (21, 'Feb 11')]
for idx, date_str in key_dates:
    ax1.annotate(date_str, (RA_deg[idx], Dec_deg[idx]),
          xytext=(0, 15), textcoords='offset points',
          fontsize=9, ha='center',
          bbox=dict(boxstyle='round,pad=0.3', facecolor='yellow', alpha=0.7),
          arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle='->', connectionstyle='arc3,rad=0'))

ax1.invert_xaxis()
ax1.set_xlabel('Right Ascension (degrees)', fontsize=12)
ax1.set_ylabel('Declination (degrees)', fontsize=12)
ax1.set_title('Piazzi\'s 22 Observations of Ceres\n(Detail View)', fontsize=14, fontweight='bold')
ax1.grid(True, alpha=0.3)
ax1.set_aspect(1.0 / np.cos(np.radians(20)))

# RIGHT: Full Sky Context (MOLLWEIDE)
ax = fig.add_subplot(122, projection='mollweide')

# Convert RA from 0-360° to -180 to +180° (Mollweide convention)
# Then to radians for plotting
def ra_to_moll(ra_deg):
    ra_shifted = ra_deg - 180  # 0-360 -> -180 to +180
    return np.radians(ra_shifted)

def dec_to_moll(dec_deg):
    return np.radians(dec_deg)

# CALCULATE RANGES FIRST (this was your issue!)
ra_range = RA_deg.max() - RA_deg.min()
dec_range = Dec_deg.max() - Dec_deg.min()

# Plot grid
ra_grid_deg = np.linspace(0, 360, 360)
for dec in range(-90, 91, 30):
    ax.plot(ra_to_moll(ra_grid_deg), dec_to_moll(np.full_like(ra_grid_deg, dec)), 
            'k-', alpha=0.2, linewidth=0.5)

dec_grid = np.linspace(-90, 90, 180)
for ra in range(0, 360, 30):
    ax.plot(ra_to_moll(np.full_like(dec_grid, ra)), dec_to_moll(dec_grid), 
            'k-', alpha=0.2, linewidth=0.5)

# Highlight observation region
from matplotlib.patches import Rectangle
ra_center_moll = ra_to_moll(np.mean(RA_deg))
dec_center_moll = dec_to_moll(np.mean(Dec_deg))
ra_range_rad = np.radians(ra_range)
dec_range_rad = np.radians(dec_range)

rect = Rectangle((ra_to_moll(RA_deg.min()) - np.radians(1), 
                  dec_to_moll(Dec_deg.min()) - np.radians(1)), 
                 ra_range_rad + np.radians(2), 
                 dec_range_rad + np.radians(2),
                 linewidth=3, edgecolor='red', facecolor='red', 
                 alpha=0.3, zorder=5, transform=ax.transData)
ax.add_patch(rect)

# Celestial equator
ax.plot(ra_to_moll(ra_grid_deg), dec_to_moll(np.zeros_like(ra_grid_deg)), 
        'b--', linewidth=2, alpha=0.7, label='Celestial Equator')

# Ecliptic
ecliptic_dec = 23.44 * np.sin(np.radians(ra_grid_deg))
ax.plot(ra_to_moll(ra_grid_deg), dec_to_moll(ecliptic_dec), 
        'g--', linewidth=2, alpha=0.7, label='Ecliptic')

# Annotation
ax.annotate('Ceres\nobservations', 
            xy=(ra_center_moll, dec_center_moll),
            xytext=(0.5, 0.5), fontsize=11,
            bbox=dict(boxstyle='round,pad=0.5', facecolor='yellow', alpha=0.8),
            arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle='->', color='red', lw=2),
            ha='center', fontweight='bold')

ax.set_xlabel('Right Ascension', fontsize=12)
ax.set_ylabel('Declination', fontsize=12)
ax.set_title('Full Sky Context - Ceres Observations in Red', 
             fontsize=14, fontweight='bold', pad=20)
ax.legend(loc='upper right', fontsize=10)
ax.grid(True, alpha=0.3)

# Set tick labels
ax.set_xticklabels(['150°', '120°', '90°', '60°', '30°', '0°', 
                    '330°', '300°', '270°', '240°', '210°'])

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

The first figure above shows the trajectory of Ceres as seen by Piazzi, the astronomer who discovered it. The second figure shows the full sky and how small the region of the sky is that Piazzi was observing. Gauss had to make a prediction of where Ceres would be in the sky based on only 22 observations in this tiny region of the sky.
